subject: chemistry
title: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution and temperature
key_idea: Molecules in a gas have a spread of energies, shown by the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. Only the molecules to the right of the activation energy can react. A small rise in temperature greatly increases that fraction, so the rate rises sharply.

blocks.text: Molecules in a gas do not all have the same energy. This section covers the curve that shows the spread.

items.meaning: A curve showing how many molecules in a gas have each value of energy, at one temperature.
The energy at the peak of the curve, which more molecules have than any other energy.

items: The x axis is molecular energy. The y axis is the number (or fraction) of molecules with that energy.
The curve starts at the origin, because no molecules have zero energy.
It is skewed and never touches the x axis at high energy, so there is no maximum energy.
The area under the curve is the total number of molecules. It does not change with temperature.
The activation energy is marked on the x axis. The area to the right of Eₐ is the number of molecules that can react.
The curve starts at the origin and does not touch the x axis again.
The area under the curve is constant for a fixed number of molecules.
Only the area beyond Eₐ represents molecules that can react.

blocks.text: Raising the temperature changes the shape of the curve. This section covers how and why the rate rises.

diagram.alt: Two Maxwell–Boltzmann curves. The lower temperature curve has a higher, narrower peak at lower energy. The higher temperature curve has a lower peak further right and a longer tail. A marker shows the activation energy, with more area beyond it for the higher temperature.

items: The peak moves to the right and gets lower. The curve flattens and spreads out.
The area under both curves is the same.
The most probable energy and the mean energy both increase.
A larger proportion of molecules has energy of at least Eₐ.
Molecules also move faster, so they collide more often.
The bigger effect is that a much greater proportion of collisions are effective.
A small rise in temperature gives a large rise in the area beyond Eₐ, so the rate rises sharply.
The activation energy itself does not change.
Higher temperature: lower, wider curve with the peak further right.
More molecules have energy of at least Eₐ, so more collisions are effective.
A small temperature rise can cause a large rise in rate.

blocks.text: The effect of temperature on rate is tested by changing only the temperature. This section covers a typical method.

items.text: Use the same volume and concentration of each reactant in every run. Warm one reactant to the chosen temperature in a water bath.
Mix the reactants and start a stopwatch.
Time a fixed change, such as a mark disappearing, or measure a quantity at regular times.
Repeat at several temperatures, keeping everything else the same.
A shorter time means a faster rate. The rate is proportional to 1 ÷ time.

items: Change only the temperature and keep everything else constant.
Rate is proportional to 1 ÷ time for a fixed change.

checks.q: State two features of a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve.
checks.a: Any two of: it starts at the origin; it does not touch the x axis at high energy; the area under the curve is the total number of molecules; it has a peak at the most probable energy.

checks.q: Describe how the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve changes when the temperature is raised.
checks.a: The peak moves to the right and becomes lower. The curve spreads out. The area under the curve stays the same.

checks.q: Explain why a small increase in temperature can cause a large increase in rate.
checks.a: A much larger proportion of molecules has energy of at least the activation energy. More collisions are effective, so the rate increases greatly.

blocks.text: Use the distribution to explain how the proportion of molecules exceeding Eₐ changes, and so the rate.

items: Describe the relationship between the Boltzmann distribution and Eₐ.
The same model is used again to explain catalysts.

blocks.text: Be ready to draw and interpret distribution curves for different temperatures, and to carry out an investigation of rate against temperature.

items: Label the axes: energy on x, number of molecules on y.
Draw both curves from the origin, with the same area, the higher temperature curve lower and further right.
Mark Eₐ and shade the area beyond it on each curve.

blocks.text: Explain temperature effects in terms of both the distribution and the frequency of effective collisions.

items: Sketch the distribution and mark Eₐ.
Say that molecules collide more often at a higher temperature.
Say that a greater proportion of collisions are effective, and that this is the larger effect.
